1.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **The word that Isaiah son of Amoz saw** to introduce a new section. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new section.

Isaiah is speaking of receiving God’s message as if it were something that he **saw** with his eyes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [received]

2.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **And it will be** to continue his introduction of a new event. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. Alternate translation: [It will happen in the last days]

Isaiah is using **in the end of days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the future” or “in a future time.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in a future time]
Isaiah is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Alternate translation: [the temple of Yahweh]

The expression **will be established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [will stand]

Here, **head** represents the top or highest point of the mountains. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the top of the mountains]

The expression **it will be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God will lift it up]

Isaiah is speaking as if the nations coming to the mountain were water that would **flow** to it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and all of the nations will gather to it]

Isaiah says **all of the nations** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that very many nations will come, not necessarily every nation in the world. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [very many nations]

3.note: The word **us** in **let us go up** includes the speakers and the people they are addressing. The peoples who are speaking are using an inclusive form to encourage one another. If your language marks inclusivity on pronouns, use the inclusive form here. Alternate translation: [and let all of us go up]
The peoples are speaking of the temple of the God of Jacob as if it were a **house** in which he lived. Alternate translation: [the temple of the God of Jacob]

3.q: וְ⁠נַעֲלֶ֣ה אֶל־הַר־יְהוָ֗ה אֶל־בֵּית֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֔ב וְ⁠יֹרֵ֨⁠נוּ֙ מִ⁠דְּרָכָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠נֵלְכָ֖ה בְּ⁠אֹרְחֹתָ֑י⁠ו
3.note: Here, **that** marks **he may teach us from his ways** as the goal or purpose of **let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [that he may teach us from his ways; indeed, let us walk in his paths]

The peoples are speaking of how Yahweh wants them to live as if his commands were **his ways** that a person learns to follow. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that he may teach us his commands]

The peoples are speaking of how Yahweh wants them to live as if that were **his paths** that they could walk along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let us live the way he wants us to live]

The word **us** in **let us walk** includes the speakers and the people they are addressing. The peoples are using an inclusive form to encourage one another. If your language marks inclusivity on pronouns, use the inclusive form here.

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. In the second clause, the verb “will go out” is left unstated because it can be understood from the first clause. Alternate translation: [and the word of Yahweh will go out from Jerusalem]

Isaiah is using the term **word** to represent the message that Yahweh has communicated. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the message of Yahweh]

4.note: Here, **their swords** and **their spears** represent warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the swords they use in war … the spears they use in battle]

Here, **plowshares** and **pruning hooks** represent peaceful agriculture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [plows … pruning tools]

5.note: **House of Jacob** refers to all the people descended from Jacob, envisioned as if they were one household living together. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Jacob]

Isaiah is speaking as if living according to Yahweh’s guidance were to **walk in the light of Yahweh**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let us walk in the light that Yahweh gives]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:3.

6.note: **The house of Jacob** refers to all the people descended from Jacob, envisioned as if they were one household living together. Alternate translation: [all the descendants of Jacob]

Isaiah is using **they are full from the east** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they have adopted the practices of the eastern nations.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have filled themselves with customs from the eastern nations]

This could mean: (1) that the Israelites literally **clap** as part of a pagan ritual. Alternate translation: [they take part in a clapping ritual] or (2) “they join hands,” that is, they make bargains or alliances. Alternate translation: [they make alliances]

There is another Hebrew verb that means “suffice” that has the same consonants as the verb that the ULT translates as **clap**. That could be the verb that Isaiah is using here. Alternate translation: [and the children of foreigners suffice] or [and there are more than enough children of foreigners around]

Isaiah is using the term **children** to refer to the descendants of foreigners, that is, foreign peoples. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the people of foreign nations]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the Philistines** practice divination, so do the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they practice divination in the same manner as do the Philistines]

7.note: The expression **is filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And he fills his land with silver and gold]

Isaiah says **there is no end to his treasures** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that Israel has accumulated very great wealth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and his treasures are endless]

The expression **is filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And he fills his land with horses]

Isaiah says **and there is no end to his chariots** as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that Israel has accumulated very many chariots. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and he has more chariots than can be counted]

8.note: The expression **is filled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And idols fill his land]

The pronouns **his** and **they** both refer to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel bow down to the work of their own hands]

9.note: The expression **is humbled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [Yahweh humbles a human]
The pronoun **you** refers to Yahweh. Isaiah is speaking directly to God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but may you, Yahweh, not lift them up]

This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a polite request for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [but please do not lift them up]

10.note: Isaiah is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the terror of Yahweh]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **terror**, **splendor**, and **majesty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who terrifies, and from his glorious and majestic greatness]

11.note: Isaiah is using **The eyes of the loftiness of a human** to represent the proud attitude of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The pridefulness of people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **loftiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [of the prideful heart of]

Isaiah is speaking of people’s pride being humbled as if it were something that could physically **become low**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will become humble]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **haughtiness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [the arrogant heart of]

Isaiah is speaking of people’s haughtiness being reduced as if it were something that could physically **bow down**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will acknowledge another as greater]

The expression **will be exalted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. The UST models one way to do that.

12.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because a day]

Isaiah is using **a day is to Yahweh of Armies** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh has appointed a time of judgment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies has appointed a day]

Isaiah is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [proud people]

The expression **being lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the ones who exalt themselves]

Isaiah uses a repetitive series of clauses from these lines through to the end of verse 16. to communicate that what he is saying should be understood as comprehensive. Use a form in your language that someone would use to describe a situation that is comprehensive and overwhelming.

Isaiah is speaking of proud people as if they were physically **high** and **lifted up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who are proud … those who are arrogant]

12.q: כִּ֣י י֞וֹם לַ⁠יהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת עַ֥ל כָּל־גֵּאֶ֖ה וָ⁠רָ֑ם וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־נִשָּׂ֥א וְ⁠שָׁפֵֽל
12.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could put the information that these proud people will **become low** before the information that describes these people. Alternate translation: [For a day is to Yahweh of Armies when they will become low; it will be a day against all of the proud and the ones being high, and against all of the ones being lifted up]

13.note: Isaiah is speaking of proud people as if they were tall trees, specifically **the cedars of Lebanon** and **the oaks of Bashan**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [proud and powerful people like the cedars of Lebanon … proud and powerful people like the oaks of Bashan]

The terms **being high** and **being lifted up** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [being proud and arrogant]

The expression **being lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and arrogant]

14.note: Isaiah is speaking of proud people as if they were **mountains being high** and **hills being lifted up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all who are very proud … all who are arrogant]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:13.

15.q: וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־מִגְדָּ֣ל גָּבֹ֑הַ וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־חוֹמָ֥ה בְצוּרָֽה
15.note: Isaiah is speaking of proud and powerful people as if they were structures like a **high tower** and a **fortified wall**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and against proud and powerful people and against people who trust in their own defenses]

16.note: Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **boats** that are characterized by **delight**, meaning boats that are beautiful or desirable. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the delightful boats]

16.q: וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־אֳנִיּ֣וֹת תַּרְשִׁ֑ישׁ וְ⁠עַ֖ל כָּל־שְׂכִיּ֥וֹת הַ⁠חֶמְדָּֽה׃
16.note: Isaiah is speaking of proud and wealthy people as if they were **ships of Tarshish** and **boats of delight**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and against all of the proud, wealthy people, and against all those who live in luxury]

17.q: וְ⁠שַׁח֙ גַּבְה֣וּת הָ⁠אָדָ֔ם וְ⁠שָׁפֵ֖ל ר֣וּם אֲנָשִׁ֑ים

19.q: וּ⁠בָ֨אוּ֙ בִּ⁠מְעָר֣וֹת צֻרִ֔ים וּ⁠בִ⁠מְחִלּ֖וֹת עָפָ֑ר מִ⁠פְּנֵ֞י פַּ֤חַד יְהוָה֙ וּ⁠מֵ⁠הֲדַ֣ר גְּאוֹנ֔⁠וֹ בְּ⁠קוּמ֖⁠וֹ לַ⁠עֲרֹ֥ץ הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
19.note: The word that the ULT translates as **when** indicates that Yahweh **arises to terrify the earth** at the same time as the people **go into caves of the rocks and into holes of the ground**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [And they will go into caves of the rocks and into holes of the ground from the face of the terror of Yahweh and from the splendor of his majesty at the same time that he arises to terrify the earth]

See how you translated the abstract nouns **terror**, **splendor**, and **majesty** in 2:10.

Isaiah is using **when he arises** as a common expression of the culture to mean “when he takes action.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he acts]

Here, **the earth** represents the people who live on it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to terrify everyone on the earth]

20.note: The pronoun **they** is used in a general sense to refer to people, craftsmen who craft idols, and the pronoun **him** refers to the person who worships the idols. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which craftsmen made for the worshiper to worship]

22.note: Here, **breath is in his nose** represents the fact that a person is merely mortal and alive only because God sustains him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who has life only because God breathes into him]

The expression **is he esteemed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [do people esteem him]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that humans are not worthy of trust. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [for he is not worthy of esteem.]
